subject: Humanities
focus: Structured evaluation of conflict causes, staged rights removal, consequences and remembrance using accurate evidence and reasoned judgements.
enquiry: How do evidence and careful judgements help us evaluate the unit?

source_workbook.basis: Owner brief: LAUNCH Weekly Spring row 45. Workbook not re-read; inherited workbook provenance is retained for traceability only.

assessment_generic: Assessing week: structured evaluation and adult six-outcome review based on actual learner evidence. No automatic earlier-outcome tick, archive-use claim, emotional-performance judgement or accredited completion.

Supported: Use the four-part grid and evidence cards. An adult may read exactly. Plan one part at a time with card codes and the frame.
Keep two cause factors, the trigger, three Germany rights dates, consequences and remembrance. Use short written sections, typing or exact directed scribing.
Keep your own first attempt before seeing the model. Record help used. After a next step, make one labelled follow-up edit with a reason.
Independent: Select evidence and plan four sections. Compare the role of causes and identify the immediate trigger.
Explain the three rights steps with dates, place and effects. Evaluate consequences and remembrance, with reasons, responsibility and a limit.
Retain your first attempt, then compare the review model and respond to one next step. Keep your own judgement and label the supported revision.
Aspire: Keep the same common finish. Weigh different causes without turning one factor into a complete explanation.
Explain the limits of a Germany-specific sequence and the difference between war, removal of rights and the Holocaust. Do not rank suffering.
Use a precise judgement about why remembrance matters and what it cannot do alone. After the first attempt, revise an overclaim and explain why.

response_modes: typing in a plain offline document
sensitive_response_route: Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or more time with the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
quiet_alternative: Quiet task: put these made-up daily times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 reading; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Then sort pencil and book, cup and plate, by use. No history words or personal story are needed.
staff_care_rules: The supplied text completes this assessment. Add no imagery or survivor testimony in any form: no quotation, paraphrase, invented voice, composite, audio, video or live browsing. No individual victim name, real photograph or website address is supplied or used. Do not add stories or archive items. Any private teacher preparation using the school’s chosen memorial-day resource must be school-approved and within the same limits; no title, organisation or address is named.

Keep the dignity and full lives of people in view. Do not use imagine-you-are tasks, victim roles, historical role play, comparisons of suffering or personal family-history questions. Do not ask any learner to speak for Jewish people, survivors or a whole community. Do not invent a life story to make the topic feel personal.

Participation is thoughtful learning, not a performance of grief. Do not require a particular feeling, silence, prayer, pledge, public statement or personal disclosure. Private response, quiet listening and passing are allowed. Assess the evidence, explanation and judgement, not visible sadness, ritual or agreement with a feeling.

Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, supervising adult, quiet place and private return check before teaching. Keep both learners supervised. If a sole adult cannot supervise separate spaces, use a calm place in the room or pause the whole group while seeking usual support. Never send a learner away alone.

For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without sanction or a public explanation. Do not probe or insist on a history recap while the learner is upset. Follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures and use the appropriate private record.

Interrupt antisemitism calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Hostility towards Jewish people is unacceptable. Correct a falsehood briefly and follow school procedures. Do not debate Holocaust denial or require learners to defend victims’ rights. Victims were not responsible for their persecution.

For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset respectful listening. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid shaming or guessing motives.

A warning is a reason to learn and act carefully, not a prediction that every unfair act leads to genocide. Do not equate everyday disagreement with the Holocaust. Remembrance alone cannot prevent hatred; education, laws, institutions and human choices matter too. Learners do not carry personal responsibility for preventing genocide.

Offer the neutral quiet task and a private readiness check. It is not evidence of the evaluation outcome. Record deferred work honestly and offer a later supported return. A partner’s answer, attendance, emotional display or copied model does not establish understanding.

Keep current writing and earlier memorial work private, on paper or in a plain offline document. Do not create accounts, use online tools, search for pictures, publish, share, export or upload work, including to an evidence app. Record the work location offline and leave E unmarked. The earlier memorial plan is reviewed in place if needed; do not reproduce it in this evaluation.
context: This assessing week brings together our unit. Evaluate causes of war in Europe, the removal of rights in Germany, consequences, and why we remember. These are linked areas of study, not one single event. Use facts to explain reasons and weigh a judgement. Keep full lives, dignity and limits in view.
source_card_status: E1–E6 are new factual teaching summaries based on accepted earlier lessons. No old text, image or person’s account is copied. No survivor testimony is reproduced, paraphrased, invented or composited. These cards are an evidence bank, not primary-source extracts.

source_cards.title: Background causes and Nazi choices
source_cards.body: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919. Many people in Germany resented its terms. Nazi leaders used this anger to seek support. From 1933, they built a dictatorship and sought more territory. The treaty was one background factor. Nazi aims and decisions drove aggression; war was not automatic.

origin.part: S1 Treaty and resentment; S2 Nazi rule and expansion

source_cards.link: Weigh different factors. A background problem did not remove the responsibility of those who chose aggression.
source_cards.think: Which fact describes a background cause, and which describes a later choice?
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

source_cards.title: Failed concessions and the trigger
source_cards.body: Britain and France made concessions at Munich in September 1938, hoping to avoid war. German forces occupied more Czech lands in March 1939. Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. Britain and France declared war on 3 September after Germany did not withdraw. The invasion was the immediate trigger for wider war in Europe.

origin.part: S3 Concessions failed to stop expansion; S4 Invasion and the immediate trigger

source_cards.link: Concessions failed to stop expansion. That did not remove Nazi leaders’ responsibility for invasion. Earlier causes and the trigger played different parts.
source_cards.think: How did the invasion differ from the longer background causes?
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

source_cards.title: Rights removed through work rules
source_cards.body: A Nazi law began removing Jewish people from state jobs in Germany. Some early exceptions existed. Losing work could remove income. People wrote and enforced these unjust rules. The people targeted were not to blame.
source_cards.link: Keep the date, place and initial exceptions. This did not remove every job from every Jewish person on one day.
source_cards.think: What right and part of daily life were affected?
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

source_cards.title: Further loss of rights in stages
source_cards.date: 15 September 1935 and later rules; November 1938 | Germany
source_cards.body: The Nuremberg Laws were passed on 15 September 1935. These laws and later rules took away German Jews’ citizenship rights. The rules used false racist ideas. In November 1938, Jewish pupils were barred from public schools in Germany. Work, political rights and education were restricted through different steps.

origin.part: S3 Citizenship rights taken away; S4 Excluded from public schools

source_cards.link: These examples concern Germany. Rules and dates differed elsewhere. Choices and enforcement caused harm; the sequence was not inevitable.
source_cards.think: How do the dates show rights being removed over time?
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

source_cards.title: Consequences for lives and communities
source_cards.body: Before Nazi rule, Jewish people had varied lives. They had families, jobs, interests and communities. Loss of rights harmed work, school and social ties. The Holocaust was the Nazi-led persecution and murder of six million European Jews. Nazi allies and those who helped them took part. Other groups faced Nazi persecution and murder. Their experiences differed.

origin.part: S1 general life context; S2–S4 effects; definition

source_cards.link: Remember full lives and loss. Do not treat the war, rights laws and the Holocaust as one event. A sequence does not prove that later events had to happen.
source_cards.think: How can you explain harm with care for people’s dignity?
source_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 2 context/definition and S2–S4; Week 4 R1.
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

source_cards.title: Remembrance and responsibility today
source_cards.body: The UK marks Holocaust Memorial Day on 27 January each year. It remembers those murdered in the Holocaust, Nazi persecution and later genocides. It gives time to learn and think. Remembering can honour people and help us study choices and hate. We can learn facts with care and check claims. We can seek safe adult help if we meet abuse.

origin.part: R1–R3 purposes; R5 national day; R6 education

source_cards.link: A day or ceremony cannot stop hate alone. Society shares responsibility. A pupil need not make a pledge or face someone who is unsafe.
source_cards.think: Why do we remember? What can one day not do?
source_cards.origin_label: Earlier learning: Week 4 R1–R3/R5/R6; Week 5 F6.
source_cards.label: Evidence for evaluation

model: Rights in Germany were removed in steps. The law of 7 April 1933 began to remove Jewish people from state jobs. Some early exceptions existed (E3). Laws passed on 15 September 1935 and later rules removed citizenship rights. In November 1938, Jewish pupils were barred from public schools (E4). Loss of work could remove income. School exclusion harmed learning and social ties. The pattern matters because it shows repeated human choices. However, these are examples from Germany, not all of Europe.

hinge.question: Which answer is an evaluation? A: A list of dates with no reasons. B: A judgement using evidence, explained links and a limit. C: A statement that everyone must feel the same sadness.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: B, with a reason about evidence and judgement. A is chronology without weighing. C assesses emotion rather than understanding. If needed, rephrase the method without supplying a historical answer. Record any reasoning support before the first attempt.
hinge.parallel: A response says one restriction happened before another, so the later harm was inevitable. Does order alone prove that? No. Ask for evidence, human choices and a limit. Record any prompt that supplies the judgement.

pair_work: Pair roles may check instructions and method only, not supply historical answers. Each learner completes an own first attempt with recorded support. A partner’s answer does not establish both outcomes.

slides.notes:
The supplied text completes this assessment. Add no imagery or survivor testimony in any form: no quotation, paraphrase, invented voice, composite, audio, video or live browsing. No individual victim name, real photograph or website address is supplied or used. Do not add stories or archive items. Any private teacher preparation using the school’s chosen memorial-day resource must be school-approved and within the same limits; no title, organisation or address is named.
Keep the dignity and full lives of people in view. Do not use imagine-you-are tasks, victim roles, historical role play, comparisons of suffering or personal family-history questions. Do not ask any learner to speak for Jewish people, survivors or a whole community. Do not invent a life story to make the topic feel personal.
Participation is thoughtful learning, not a performance of grief. Do not require a particular feeling, silence, prayer, pledge, public statement or personal disclosure. Private response, quiet listening and passing are allowed. Assess the evidence, explanation and judgement, not visible sadness, ritual or agreement with a feeling.
Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, supervising adult, quiet place and private return check before teaching. Keep both learners supervised. If a sole adult cannot supervise separate spaces, use a calm place in the room or pause the whole group while seeking usual support. Never send a learner away alone.
For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without sanction or a public explanation. Do not probe or insist on a history recap while the learner is upset. Follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements for disclosures and use the appropriate private record.
Interrupt antisemitism calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Hostility towards Jewish people is unacceptable. Correct a falsehood briefly and follow school procedures. Do not debate Holocaust denial or require learners to defend victims’ rights. Victims were not responsible for their persecution.
For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset respectful listening. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid shaming or guessing motives.
A warning is a reason to learn and act carefully, not a prediction that every unfair act leads to genocide. Do not equate everyday disagreement with the Holocaust. Remembrance alone cannot prevent hatred; education, laws, institutions and human choices matter too. Learners do not carry personal responsibility for preventing genocide.
